title: Base Models Know How to Reason, Thinking Models Learn When
claim: A base model's capabilities plus a learned classifier for when to fire a steering vector can recover the thinking model's behavior.
layout: 3 stacked rows, top-to-bottom, lettered A/B/C callouts, dotted arrow linking classifier to steering
description: A token-level diagram on a white background. The top row shows an input prompt as grey token boxes (a math word problem about vacuum cleaners), with a user icon labeled Input. Below it, row A shows the Base model generating purple tokens ('Okay, so I have this math problem...') followed by yellow arithmetic tokens ('So x = 5.'). From there, two arrows lead to the next token. The unsteered path gives a red 'Answer:' box marked with a red X. The path labeled C, '+backtracking steering vector', gives a green 'Wait' box marked with a green check. Row B shows the Thinking model producing the same tokens. A rainbow 'Classifier' trapezoid sits above grey and green dots. A color-coded table at lower right gives category probabilities: Backtracking 85%, Uncertainty Estimation 10%, Arithmetic 5%, and 0% for the rest. A dotted arrow carries the chosen category up to the steering vector.
caption: Constructive Model Diffing for Thinking LLMs. We decompose the difference between base and thinking models into two interpretable components. (A) The base model generates tokens, providing the underlying reasoning capabilities. (B) A reasoning heuristic, extracted from the thinking model via SAE activations, determines when to deploy each reasoning mechanism. (C) Category vectors, optimized in the base model, induce the corresponding reasoning behavior when triggered. If this explicit construction recovers the thinking model's performance, it provides evidence that the diff is well-characterized by our decomposition: the thinking model learned sophisticated heuristics over pre-existing base model mechanisms.
abstract: What do thinking language models learn during training that their base models lack? We first present an unsupervised method that discovers a model's reasoning behaviors by training small Sparse Autoencoders on sentence-level activations of reasoning traces, yielding interpretable reasoning taxonomies. Building on this, we introduce constructive model diffing, which aims to reconstruct the base-to-fine-tuned difference from interpretable components: reasoning mechanisms (category vectors that can induce a reasoning behavior in the base model) and reasoning heuristics (a classifier determining when a mechanism should fire). Across nine base/thinking pairs (four RL-trained, four SFT-distilled, one mixed), two independent findings agree: category vectors in the base model converge to far lower loss for taxonomies derived from purely RL-trained models, and hybrid models recover roughly 76% of the RL base-to-thinking gap but only 11% of the SFT gap. This indicates RL primarily teaches heuristics for orchestrating pre-existing base mechanisms, whereas SFT-distillation installs new ones, offering a new lens on what training paradigms teach, with implications for efficient reasoning-model development.
